statement: Four villages A, B, C and D lie along one straight road. B is 5 km from A, C is 3 km from B, D is 7 km from C, and D is 9 km from A. How far is C from A, in km?

choices.misconception: I put the villages in the order A, B, C and added 5 + 3, without checking that D can then be 9 km from A.
I put C 7 km beyond D, so 9 + 7, and did not check whether B could then be 5 km from A and 3 km from C.
I found the right order but gave the distance from B to C instead of from A to C.
I found the two places 7 km from D, at 2 km and at 16 km from A, and did not use the clues about B to rule one of them out.

hints: Draw the road as a line and put A at 0.
Place the villages using the clues one at a time. Fix A and D first, since their distance is given, then find the possible places for C, and test each against the clues about B.
With A at 0 and D at 9, C is at 2 or at 16. Only one of these is 3 km from a point 5 km from A.

solutions.reliable: Put A at 0 on the road and D at 9. C is 7 km from D, so C is at 2 or at 16. B is 5 km from A, so B is at 5 or at negative 5. B must also be 3 km from C: the point 5 is 3 km from 2, while neither 5 nor negative 5 is 3 km from 16. So C is at 2, and the order along the road is A, C, B, D. C is 2 km from A. The transferable idea: place the most definite clues first, list the few possible positions, and test each one against every remaining clue.

whyOnTest: Ordering from clues rewards drawing the line and testing every case, and the wrong choices come from assuming the order the letters are listed in.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
